opus-5.5.text:
I think they're deeply intertwined, and increasingly I see them as two views of the same underlying capability. When we talk about reasoning, especially the "thinking" style of models that spend more compute at inference time, what we're really building is a model that can take a hard problem, break it down, try things, notice when it's gone wrong, and course-correct. That's exactly the skill set you need to be a good agent.

Early reasoning work focused on domains like math and competitive programming, partly because they have clean, verifiable answers. You can tell whether the model got it right, so you have a strong training signal. But the behaviors that emerge there, like planning, backtracking, self-verification, and persistence over long chains of thought, aren't really about math. They're general problem-solving behaviors, and they transfer.

Agentic settings add a couple of things. The model is interacting with an environment, calling tools, reading results, and dealing with a world that doesn't always behave the way it expected. The horizon is also much longer: instead of thinking for a few minutes about a single problem, you might be operating over hours across many steps. So the reasoning has to be interleaved with action. You think, you act, you observe, you think again.

So I'd say reasoning is the core cognitive engine and agentic research is about connecting that engine to the world and making it robust over long horizons. Some of the most exciting progress comes from training them together, because when a model has to actually accomplish something in an environment, you get a richer and more grounded signal about whether its reasoning was any good. Over time I expect the distinction to blur. We'll just be thinking about models that can think and act effectively toward a goal.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes reasoning as the cognitive engine from agentic research that connects it to the world and focuses on action, while describing them as intertwined.

r002.rationale: It discusses agents interacting with environments, but does not identify creating environments for agents as a separate research area.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think they're really deeply intertwined, and honestly I'd say that over the past year or so the distinction has become a lot blurrier than it used to be. If you go back to when we started thinking seriously about reasoning, thinking models, test-time compute, the framing was very much about a single problem: you give the model a hard math question or a coding problem, it thinks for a while, and it produces an answer. The whole thing was fairly self-contained. Agentic behavior felt like a somewhat separate line of work, more about tool use, taking actions in an environment, operating over long horizons.

But what you quickly realize is that reasoning is kind of the engine that makes agentic behavior actually work. An agent that can't plan, can't reflect on whether its last action succeeded, can't notice it's gone down a wrong path and back out, is going to be pretty brittle. All of that is reasoning. It's just reasoning that's happening interleaved with actions rather than in one big block before a final answer. So I tend to think of agentic tasks as reasoning tasks with a different shape. The thinking is spread out over time, it has to incorporate new information coming back from the world, and the model has to decide not just what to conclude but what to do next and when it has enough information to stop.

And it goes the other direction too. Agentic settings are turning out to be one of the best places to actually develop and evaluate reasoning. In a closed-form math problem you get one verifiable signal at the end. In an agentic environment you get a whole stream of feedback, and the model has to be good at reasoning under uncertainty, at calibrating how confident it is, at knowing when to go check something rather than guess. Those are capabilities that are hard to even surface in the static setting. So a lot of the hardest open reasoning problems, things like long-horizon coherence, error recovery, knowing what you don't know, really only become visible once you put the model in an agentic loop.

So in practice, at least the way I think about it, they're not really two research programs anymore. The methods are converging, the training signals are converging, and increasingly the question is just: how do we get models to think well over long stretches of time, where "thinking" includes both the internal deliberation and the external actions. I'd expect that convergence to keep going.

r001.rationale: The response describes agentic behavior as having felt like a somewhat separate line of work focused on tool use and taking actions in an environment.

r002.rationale: The response discusses using agentic environments to develop and evaluate reasoning, but does not identify creating those environments as a separable research area.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re very closely related. Reasoning is useful when you need to work through a problem before giving an answer, and agentic behavior extends that to situations where you can take actions, observe what happens, and adjust your approach. In both cases, you’re asking: how do we use a sequence of steps to achieve a better outcome?

The difference is that, for an agent, some of those steps change the outside world. You might run some code, inspect the result, and discover that an assumption was wrong. So the challenge isn’t just making a good plan; it’s knowing when to gather more information, when to act, and when to revise the plan.

I’d expect progress in the two areas to reinforce each other. Better reasoning should help agents make better decisions, while working on agents gives us a way to test whether that reasoning actually holds up when there’s feedback and uncertainty.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes agentic behavior from reasoning by describing agents taking actions, observing outcomes, and revising plans.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention creating environments for agents as a research area.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re very closely related. Reasoning is one of the things you want an agent to be able to do, but an agent also has to decide when to reason, when to take an action, and when to get more information from the environment.

If you think about a model solving a problem, it can spend more time thinking internally, or it can run some code, look something up, or ask a question. Those are all ways of making progress. The interesting question is how it learns to allocate its effort between them.

And both settings involve this challenge of credit assignment over a long sequence: you make a decision now, and perhaps much later you find out whether it was useful. So I expect a lot of the techniques that improve reasoning to help with agentic behavior as well. But being good at a self-contained reasoning problem doesn’t automatically make you a reliable agent. Once you’re interacting with an environment, you need to handle uncertainty, notice when something has gone wrong, and adapt your plan.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes agent behavior from self-contained reasoning by describing decisions about when to reason, act, or gather information, and the additional demands of interacting with an environment.

r002.rationale: It discusses agents interacting with environments, but does not identify creating environments for agents as a separate research area.
